title: Multiplication formula for Hernandez and Leclerc's quivers with potentials

snippets.content: In this paper, we study multiplication formula of F-polynomial of representations of Hernandez and Leclerc's quivers with potentials. Since the truncated q-characters of some real simple modules over a quantum affine group U_q(ĝ) can be expressed in terms of such F-polynomials, one can describe the product of two simple modules over U_q(ĝ) using this multiplication formula.

Consider a simple Lie algebra g. The quantum affine algebra for g, denoted as U_q(ĝ), holds significant importance across various disciplines. Central to understanding representations of U_q(ĝ) is the concept of q-characters, introduced by Frenkel and Reshetikhin [FR98]. However, detailing the q-characters of all simple modules over U_q(ĝ) proves intricate. To address this complexity, Hernandez and Leclerc introduced the truncated q-character for simple modules over U_q(ĝ) [HL10]. Subsequently, they expressed these truncated q-characters of Kirillov–Reshetikhin modules in terms of F-polynomials of modules over their quivers Q_HL with potentials [HL16]. Extending this to a broader class of simple modules over U_q(ĝ), Kashiwara, Kim, Oh, and Park demonstrated that the truncated q-characters of real simple modules corresponding to cluster monomials can be described using F-polynomials of representations of Q_HL with potentials [KKOP24]. Consequently, understanding the product of real simple modules over U_q(ĝ) necessitates examining the product of F-polynomials of two corresponding representations of Q_HL with potentials. On a separate note, the multiplication formula has garnered attention from numerous experts [CK08, GLS07, Pal12, XX09, KPQ23]. However, much of the focus lies on triangular categories or 2-Calabi–Yau categories. In this study, we delve into the category of representations of Q_HL with potentials. It's worth mentioning that Q_HL can be identified with the Gabriel quiver of an endomorphism ring of a tilting object T of the Frobenius category of modules over a preprojective algebra. However, whether this endomorphism ring is the Jacobian algebra for Q_HL remains unknown, rendering our findings novel. As a result, we establish a connection between the head of the product of two real simple modules and the generic extension of modules over the Jacobian algebra for Q_HL, akin to [LM21, Conjecture 5.1].
The author expresses gratitude to Professor Fan Qin for engaging discussions and valuable insights.

In this section, we delve into the representations of quivers with potentials as introduced in [HL16]. Let C = (c_ij)_{i,j ∈ I} represent an indecomposable n × n Cartan matrix of finite type. Accompanying C, there exists a diagonal matrix D = (d_i)_{i ∈ I} such that their product, denoted as B = DC = (b_ij)_{i,j ∈ I}, yields a symmetric matrix. For the purposes of this paper, we assume C to be simply-laced, implying its symmetry, where C = B. Here, I signifies the vertex set of the associated quiver linked to the Cartan matrix C, and r denotes the lacing number of g.

Before introducing Hernandez and Leclerc's quiver, let's revisit a semi-infinite quiver. For further elaboration, we refer readers to [HL16]. Define Ṽ = I × ℤ, introducing a quiver Γ̃ with the vertex set Ṽ. Following [HL16], Γ̃ encompasses two isomorphic connected components, of which we select one and term it Γ. The vertex set of Γ is denoted by V. For further analysis, we adopt a secondary labeling of the vertices of Γ. This labeling is derived from the initial one through the function ψ defined as ψ(i, r) = (i, r + d_i), ((i, r) ∈ V). Let W ⊂ I × ℤ denote the image of V under ψ. Γ can thus be denoted by G with vertices labeled by W. Define W⁻ := W ∩ (I × ℤ_{≤0}), and let G⁻ be the full subquiver of G with the vertex set W⁻. Consider an infinite set of indeterminates z⁻ = {z_{i,r} | (i, r) ∈ W⁻} over ℚ. Let A denote the cluster algebras defined by the initial seed (z⁻, G⁻). Define V⁻ := ψ^{-1}(W⁻), and denote by Γ⁻ the full subquiver of Γ with the vertex set V⁻. For every i ≠ j in I with c_ij ≠ 0, and every (i, m) in V⁻, we observe in Γ⁻ an oriented cycle. We establish a potential S as the formal sum of all these oriented cycles up to cyclic permutations, referencing [DWZ08]. Let R represent the list of all cyclic derivatives of S. Define J as the two-sided ideal of the path algebras ℂΓ⁻ generated by R. Let A denote the infinite-dimensional ℂ-algebra ℂΓ⁻/J.

Consider a finite quiver Q̃ = (Q̃_0, Q̃_1, s, t) associated with any g... We equip the quiver Q̃ with a bigrading. Next, choose a sign ω_ij ∈ {-1, 1} for i ∼ j such that ω_ij = -ω_ji. Define the k-algebra Π as the quotient of kQ̃ by relations. We naturally identify a graded module M over the path algebra kQ̃ with a graded representation of Q̃. This functor induces an isomorphism of categories, as given by [FM23]: Φ : Π̃-gmod ≅ A-mod. We present some fundamental properties of Π̃-gmod. Define ε = ∑ ε_i^{r/d} e_i and the algebra Π(l) = Π̃/ε^l Π̃.

In this section, we aim to realize the algebra A as the endomorphism ring of a tilting module over the preprojective algebra of Q. For detailed discussions, we refer readers to [KKOP24]. Let w_0 represent the longest element of the Weyl group of g, and let w_0 = s_{i_1}⋯s_{i_l} be a reduced expression of w_0. We extend the definition of (i_k)_{k∈[1,l]} to (i_k)_{k∈ℤ}. A function ξ : I → ℤ is termed a height function on the Dynkin diagram Δ if it satisfies |ξ_i - ξ_j| = 1 for i ∼ j. From a height function on Δ, we can construct a Dynkin quiver Q. We can select Γ as the component of Γ̃ such that Î ⊂ Γ. Let Φ̂ := Φ⁺ × ℤ, where Φ⁺ is the set of positive roots. According to [HL15], there exists a bijection φ : Î → Φ̂. Let I_ξ denote the inverse image φ^{-1}(Φ × 0). We say that an infinite sequence c := (i_k, p_k)_{k∈ℤ} in I × ℤ is admissible if certain conditions are satisfied. For a sequence c of w_0, let us define Q_GLS(w_0) as the quiver structure on ℤ with vertical and horizontal arrows. According to [KKOP24, Proposition 7.27], the bijection ℤ → Î yields an isomorphism Q_GLS(c) ≃ Γ. We define the subquiver Q⁻_GLS(c) as the inverse image of Γ⁻. The cluster algebra A is identified with the cluster algebra with initial seed ((z_k)_{k∈ℤ_{≤0}}, Q_GLS(c), ℤ_{≤0}). Following [KKOP24, Definition 4.14], we say that c = [a, b] is i-box if -∞ < a ≤ b < +∞ and i_a = i_b.

Let M denote a finite-dimensional module over the algebra A, and let e be a dimension vector in ℕ[V⁻]. The variety Gr_e(M) represents submodules of M with dimension vector e, and χ(Gr_e(M)) denotes its Euler characteristic. Inspired by [DWZ10], we introduce the polynomial F_M. Consider two modules M_1 and M_2 of A. Building on [DWZ10], we find that F_{M_1}F_{M_2} = F_{M_1⊕M_2}.

This section focuses on proving our multiplication formula. First, let's review some facts about extension groups of modules over A. Let D(M_1, M_2) denote K̃er f_{M_1, M_2} as in [GLS17, formula (12.5)]. We decompose D(M_1, M_2) into Im g̃_{M_1, M_2} ⊕ E(M_1, M_2). Notably, Ext¹_Π(M_1, M_2) ≅ E(M_1, M_2). Using isomorphism (2.4), we derive Ext¹_A(M_1, M_2) ≅ D Ext¹_A(M_2, M_1). From here on, let E(M_1, M_2) ≅ Ext¹_A(M_1, M_2). Consider an extension η of M_1 and M_2, and let m(η) be the corresponding module over A, forming a short exact sequence η: 0 → M_2 → m(η) → M_1 → 0. For a dimension vector β such that β ≤ dim m(η) = γ, define Gr_β(m(η)). Choosing a decomposition W⊕T = V with dim V = γ and dim W = dim M_2, we express m(η) as a tuple of matrices x_h. For any W' ∈ Gr_β(m(η)), define subspaces W'_2 = W'∩W, W'_1 = W'/W'∩W. This induces a map q_η. To understand the map q_η, recall the map p sending W' to (V'/W∩V', W∩V'). For a pair vector space (T', W'), p^{-1}(T', W') = Hom_I(T', W/W'). For an element z in Hom_I(T', W/W'), define V_z = (W',0) + {(z(t), t) | t ∈ T'}. If there exists a short exact sequence 0 → W' → V' → T' → 0, it yields a map z ∈ Hom_I(T', V'/W') such that V' = (W', 0) + {(z(t), t) | t ∈ T'}. Hence, we obtain formula (3.6).

snippets.content: Let g be the simple Lie algebra over ℂ. We denote by α_i (i ∈ I) the simple roots of g, and by ω_i the fundamental weights of g. Let ĝ be the corresponding untwisted affine Lie algebra and U_q(ĝ) be the Drinfeld-Jimbo quantum enveloping algebra of ĝ, see e.g. [CP95]. Frenkel and Reshetikhin [FR98] have attached to every complex finite-dimensional representation M of U_q(ĝ) a q-character χ_q(M). By definition, the q-character χ_q(M) is a Laurent polynomial with positive integer coefficients in the infinite set of variables Y = {Y_{i,a} | i ∈ I, a ∈ ℂ*}, which should be seen as a quantum affine analogue of {e^{ω_i} | i ∈ I}. Let m be a dominant monomial in the variables Y_{i,r} ∈ Y, that is, a monomial with nonnegative exponents. We denote by L(m) the corresponding irreducible representation of U_q(ĝ), and by χ_q(m) = χ_q(L(m)) its q-character. For example, if m is of the form (4.1), L(m) is called Kirillov-Reshetikhin module, and usually denoted by W^{(i)}_{k,r}. C⁻ denotes the monomial subcategory of modules generated by fundamental module V_{i,a} for all (i, a) ∈ Γ⁻. Following [FR98], for (i, r) ∈ V we introduce the quantum affine analogue of e^{α_i}: A_{i,r}. To relate the q-character of simple modules with the F-polynomials for the algebra A, we need more notations. Let Y⁻ = {Y_{i,r} ∈ Y | (i, r) ∈ W⁻}. For (i, r) ∈ W⁻, we perform the substitution z_{i,r} = ∏_{k≥0, r+kb_{ii}≤0} Y_{i,r+kb_{ii}}. In the sequel, we shall evaluate the variables of the F-polynomials as the inverses of the variables A_{i,r} introduced in (4.2), namely: v_{i,r} = A_{i,r}^{-1}. Our F-polynomials are given by the equation (3.1). Next, we will introduce a class of modules over A: Let I_{i,m} be the (infinite-dimensional) injective A-module with socle isomorphic to S_{i,m}. The ℂ-vector space I_{i,m} has a basis indexed by classes modulo J of paths in Γ⁻ with final vertex (i, m). Let K^{(i)}_{k,m} be the kernel of a generic A-module homomorphism from I_{i,m} to I_{i,m-kb_{ii}}. One also defines such modules on generalized preprojective algebra Π̃. For each i ∈ I and k ∈ ℤ_{>0}, we define the graded Π̃-module K^{(i)}_k. From the definition, the module K^{(i)}_k fits into a short exact sequence. Following [FM23, Remark 5.2], we obtain Φ(q^{r-kd_i}K^{(i)}_k) = K^{(i)}_{k,r}.
In order to prove theorem 2.3, we need a lemma. Following [KKOP24], we say that i-boxes [a1, b1] and [a2, b2] commute if we have either a1⁻ < a2 ≤ b2 < b1⁺ or a2⁻ < a1 ≤ b1 < b2⁺.

snippets.content: Proposition 2.1. Let M and N be two modules over Π̃, locally free over Π(l) for some l, then we have: Ext_A^1(Φ(M), Φ(N)) = D Ext_A^1(Φ(N), Φ(M)).

Definition 2.2. For an i-box c = [a, b], one can define the module M[a, b] as the generic kernel of maps Hom_A(I_{(i_a,p_a)}, I_{(i_b,p_b)}), namely, 0 → M[a,b] → I_{(i_a,p_a)} → I_{(i_b,p_b)} → 0. By the isomorphism (2.4) and [FM23, Proposition 5.1], M[a,b] is equal to the image of q^{p_a}K^{(i_a)}_{(p_a-p_b)/2} under the map Φ.

Theorem 2.3. Consider a ξ-adapted admissible sequence c in Ĩ_g and a ∈ ℤ, we set the module M[a,0]. The module M^{-∞} := ⊕_{a∈ℤ_{<0}} M[a,0] is a rigid module, and the Gabriel quiver Q^{-∞} of the endomorphism ring End_A(M^{-∞}) equals Q_{GLS}.
Conjecture 2.4. We conjecture that End_A(M^{-∞}) is the Jacobian algebra for Q_{GLS} with the potential (2.2).
Remark 2.5. If the above conjecture holds, then our multiplication formula 3.2 is a consequence of the results of [KPQ23].

Lemma 3.1. Given a pair of vector spaces (T', W'), for an element z ∈ Hom_I(T', W/W') we have V_z ∈ Gr_β(m(η)) if and only if x_{2,h}z(t) - z x_{1,h}(t) + u_h(t) ∈ W' for all t ∈ T'. Moreover, q_η^{-1}(T', W') = ∅ or q_η^{-1}(T', W') is isomorphic to an affine space.

Theorem 3.2. Let M_1, M_2 be two modules over A, then χ(ℙExt_A^1(M_1, M_2)) F_{M_1}·F_{M_2} = ∑_Y (χ(ℙExt_A^1(M_1, M_2)_Y) + χ(ℙExt_A^1(M_2, M_1)_Y)) F_Y. In particular, when Ext¹_A(M_1, M_2) = 1, we obtain F_{M_1}·F_{M_2} = F_{Y_1} + F_{Y_2}.

[HL16, Theorem 5.1; Conjecture 5.2] The cluster algebra A is identified with the image of the injective ring homomorphism from K_0(C⁻) to ℤ[Y_{i,r} | (i,r) ∈ Y⁻] given by L(m) ↦ χ_q⁻(m). Moreover, the cluster monomials get identified with the truncated q-characters of real simple modules. Note that the last statement was proved by Kashiwara, Kim, Oh and Park in [KKOP24].

snippets.content: Proposition 4.3. Let m_1, m_2 be two cluster monomials in A, L_1, L_2 be corresponding simple modules over U_q(ĝ), and M_1, M_2 be the corresponding rigid modules over A. The tensor product L_1 ⊗ L_2 is simple if and only if Ext_A^1(M_1, M_2) = 0.
Lemma 4.4. If two i-boxes [a_1,b_1] and [a_2,b_2] commute, then Ext_A^1(M[a_1,b_1], M[a_2,b_2]) = 0.

Theorem 4.5. For any two real simple modules L_1, L_2 over U_q(ĝ) for two cluster monomials m_1, m_2, let M_1 and M_2 be the rigid module over A for m_1, m_2. If the head of L_1⊗L_2 is a simple module corresponding to some cluster monomial m, then its corresponding module M over A is the generic extension M_1 by M_2 or M_2 by M_1, namely, M = M_1 * M_2 or M = M_2 * M_1.
Remark 4.6. This theorem gives an answer to the [LM21, Conjecture 5.1] in the sense of generalized preprojective algebras.
Proof of Proposition 2.1. This follows from the isomorphism Φ and [GLS17, Theorem 1.8]: Ext¹_{Π̃}(M, N) ≅ D Ext¹_{Π̃}(N, M). □

Proof of Lemma 3.1. By equation (3.4), the condition x(V_z) ⊂ V_z is equivalent to (x_{2,h}z - zx_{1,h} + u_h)|_{T'} = 0 in W/W'. This proves the claim. If q_η^{-1}(T', W') ≠ ∅, any two z_1, z_2 ∈ q_η^{-1}(T', W') satisfy (x_{2,h}(z_1-z_2) - (z_1-z_2)x_{1,h})(T') ⊂ W'. It implies z_1 - z_2 ∈ Hom_A(M_2, M_1|_{W/W'}). Hence, q_η^{-1}(T', W') ≅ Hom_A(M_2, M_1|_{W/W'}). □

Proof of Theorem 3.2. Let L_1 be the image of q. Define EF(M_1, M_2) and ψ. Following [Dim04, Proposition 4.1.31], ℙE(M_1, M_2) can be decomposed. By [GLS07, Proposition 7.4.1], χ(EF(M_1, M_2)) = ∑_Y χ(Gr_β(m(Y)))χ(ℙE(M_1,M_2)_{⟨Y⟩}). Consider Φ : EF(M_1,M_2) → ⊔ ℙE(M_1,M_2)×Gr_{β_1}(M_1)×Gr_{β_2}(M_2). For any (η,T',W') ∈ L_1, fiber Φ⁻¹(η,T',W') = q_η⁻¹(T',W') = affine space, so χ(EF(M_1,M_2)) = χ(L_1). Let L_2 be complement of L_1. Define C. Fix (T', W') ∈ Im q_η. By [GLS07], E(M_1,M_2)^⊥_{T',W'} = E(M_2,M_1)_{W',T'}. Map C→L_2 surjective with affine fibers, so χ(L_2)=χ(C). Map pr: C→EF(M_2,M_1) has affine fibers, so χ(C)=χ(EF(M_2,M_1)). Summing up yields (3.16). In particular, when Ext¹_A(M_1,M_2)=1, F_{M_1}·F_{M_2} = F_{Y_1}+F_{Y_2} where Y_1 subjects to 0→M_1→Y_1→M_2→0 and Y_2 subjects to 0→M_2→Y_2→M_1→0. □

snippets.content: Proof of Proposition 4.3. If L_1⊗L_2 is a simple module, then there exists a rigid module T over A such that F_{M_1}·F_{M_2} = F_T and g_T = g_{M_1} + g_{M_2}. It implies that there exists a short exact sequence 0→M_1→T→M_2→0 or 0→M_2→T→M_1→0. If Ext_A^1(M_1, M_2) ≠ 0, then by theorem 3.2, we get χ(ℙExt_A^1(M_1,M_2))F_T = ∑_Y(χ(ℙExt_A^1(M_1,M_2)_Y)+χ(ℙExt_A^1(M_2,M_1)_Y))F_Y. Since T appears in the right hand of the above equation, we have Y=T for all Y in the right hand, which implies F_T = 2F_T. It is a contradiction. If Ext_A^1(M_1, M_2) = 0, then M_1⊕M_2 is rigid. The truncated q-character of L_1⊗L_2 is equal to z^{g_1+g_2}F_{M_1⊕M_2} which is a cluster monomial. It means L_1⊗L_2 is simple. □

Proof of Theorem 4.5. Since χ_q⁻(L_i)=z^{g_i}F_{M_i} for any i=1,2, we get χ_q⁻(L_1)·χ_q⁻(L_2) = z^{g_1+g_2}F_{M_1⊕M_2}. If the head of L_1⊗L_2 is a monomial simple module, then ∃ rigid module T: χ_q⁻(L_1⊗L_2) = χ_q⁻(L_1)·χ_q⁻(L_2) = z^{g'}F_T+P for some P. The dominant monomial of L_1⊗L_2 is unique, so g'=g_1+g_2. [Second Proof block:] Following [KKOP24, Definition 4.14], for any i-box [a,b], they define the determinantal module M[a,b] over U_q(ĝ). Using [HL16, Theorem 4.18] and [KKOP24, Theorem 8.2], χ_q⁻(M[a,b])=z^gF_M. The dominant monomial for M[a,b] equals ∏ Y_{i,p_a+kb_i}=z_{i_a,p_a}/z_{i_b,p_b}. g is identified with g_{i_k,p_k}=1 if k=a, -1 if k=b, 0 otherwise. Following [DWZ10], M is the generic kernel of I_{i_a,p_a}→I_{i_b,p_b}→0, equal to M[a,b] by our definition. By [KKOP24, Theorem 4.21], M[a_1,b_1]⊗M[a_2,b_2] is real simple. Using Proposition 4.3, Ext_A^1(M[a_1,b_1],M[a_2,b_2])=0. □

Proof of Theorem 2.3. Following the above Lemma and [KKOP24, Theorem 7.20], M^{-∞} is a tilting module over A. We will calculate the Gabriel quiver of End_A(M^{-∞}). It is directly deduced from [BIRS09, Theorem II.4.1]. □ It follows that 0→M_i→I_1^{g_i⁻}→I_2^{g_i⁺}→0 for each i=1,2 and 0→T→I_1^{g'_-}→I_2^{g'_+}→0. It is easy to see that there exists an exact sequence 0→M_{L_1}→T→M_{L_2}→0 or 0→M_{L_2}→T→M_{L_1}→0. Since T is a rigid module, it follows that T=M_1*M_2 or T=M_2*M_1. □

Proof of Lemma 4.4. Following [KKOP24, Definition 4.14], for any i-box [a,b], they define the determinantal module M[a,b] over U_q(ĝ). Using [HL16, Theorem 4.18] and [KKOP24, Theorem 8.2], χ_q⁻(M[a,b])=z^gF_M. g is identified with g_{i_k,p_k}=1 if k=a, -1 if k=b, 0 otherwise. M is the generic kernel equal to M[a,b]. By [KKOP24, Theorem 4.21], the tensor product M[a_1,b_1]⊗M[a_2,b_2] is real simple. Using Proposition 4.3, Ext_A^1(M[a_1,b_1],M[a_2,b_2])=0. □
